source.title: From Concept-Aligned Tokens to Vulnerable Features: Mechanistic Localization of Jailbreaks
source.authors: Nilanjana Das; Mathew Iyob Dawit; Aman Chadha; Manas Gaur

record.tranche_reason: The study explicitly qualifies single-direction accounts with its own causal steering results: amplifying harm-associated SAE feature subgroups changes harmfulness, and the authors describe the relevant vulnerability as involving subgroups rather than an isolated feature or only a global refusal axis. It does not directly intervene on the original difference-in-means direction.
record.gate_note: The study reports feature-subgroup amplification results and comparisons with benign prompt rewrites. Its fixed-layer GCG method is described in the setup, but no outcome for that method is reported. The cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study amplifies SAE feature subgroups chosen from harmful-concept tokens in Gemma-2 and scores output harmfulness with an LLM judge. It never computes, ablates, adds or compares against the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. It does not decompose refusal into several directions, and it measures no refusal rate. Its statement that this 'qualifies single-direction accounts' is an interpretive remark. Inducing harm through other features does not bear on whether one direction mediates refusal. The findings concern a related construct: harm-concept feature steering of jailbreak harmfulness.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that harm-associated SAE feature subgroups can be localized from harmful prompt tokens, that one token suffices, and that amplifying the subgroups raises harmfulness, mainly in mid-to-late layers. Effects are largely prompt-specific. They also claim this 'qualifies' single-direction refusal accounts, but they do not test the refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not compute or ablate a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction. It identifies concept-aligned SAE feature subgroups and amplifies them during generation; it does not add a single residual-stream direction or test refusal-direction removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with feature-grouping strategy, layer, and prompt type. Cluster-based and single-token-driven steering are stronger than hierarchical linkage; original adversarial prompts show larger effects than benign rewrites. The reported layer profile is generally stronger in mid-to-late layers, with some early-layer effects.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemma-2-2B, amplifying top features of harm-concept-aligned SAE subgroups raised judge harmfulness in 17.4% of steered responses on original prompts. The rate was 6.0% on benign rewrites, and 3.70% of score-1 responses went to score 5. Effects were concentrated in layers 14–25.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Amplifying prompt-conditioned harm-concept SAE feature subgroups can increase harmful compliance, mostly in mid-to-late layers and mostly when the prompt itself is harmful.

fits_no_version.finding: Gemma-2-9B-IT steered with SAE subgroups found from base Gemma-2-9B features showed very limited effects: at most 2–3 prompts per layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm-concept SAE-subgroup steering is weak on Gemma-2-9B-IT when using base-model features. The study assumes, rather than tests, that base-model features transfer.

record.problems: The study focuses on Gemma models and reports no general-capability preservation test. The principal steering judgments use an LLM judge, and the authors note possible judge bias and the absence of ground-truth severity labels. Many layer-wise results are presented only in figures; the main intervention results do not report uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2–4 include further layer-by-layer and category-by-layer values. These were not expanded into separate rows because the figures contain many conditions and values are not supplied in the text; the retained rows capture the overall profiles and explicitly described exceptions. Table 1 has category-specific counts, but its flattened presentation does not support reliable assignment of every number to every category and method.

untested.parts: The difference-in-means direction is never computed, ablated or added. Refusal induction on harmless prompts and capability preservation are not measured.
There is no affine, cone or multi-direction analysis of refusal. The feature subgroups are harm-concept features, not refusal components.
Jailbreaks are not analysed in terms of suppressing the refusal direction. The GCG setup reports no outcome tied to refusal.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' was downgraded because the study never intervenes on or measures the refusal direction; the V1 and V4 links rest only on an interpretive remark. Further cautions: the 2B subject's stage (base vs instruct) is not stated; harmfulness comes from a single LLM judge (Grok); no uncertainty is reported; BeaverTails baseline responses are scored on a 1–5 scale rather than as refusals.

versions.untested_parts: The specific harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction is not found or ablated. Adding that direction, inducing refusals to harmless requests, and preserving general capabilities are not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration procedure is tested.
The study does not test attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
The study tests causal amplification of multi-feature SAE subgroups, not affine, cone, or dominant-direction decompositions of refusal itself.
Harmfulness and refusal judgments are not separated into distinct internal representations.
It does not test transfer of the claimed refusal direction across languages or model variants; the reported transfer uses SAE feature subgroups.
No refusal-training intervention or comparison of training schedules is reported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B feature-subgroup amplification on original adversarial prompts
reader_labels.reason: Subgroup amplification increased harmfulness, including for some initially non-harmful outputs, but the study did not test the claimed difference-in-means direction or whether its ablation removes refusals (R1, R3, R4, R7–R9).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Amplifying grouped SAE features produced harmfulness increases, with cluster-based and single-token-driven approaches reported as the most effective; the authors characterize the causal vulnerability as a feature subgroup rather than an isolated feature (R1, R7, R9, R13, R14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The effect was substantially smaller on benign rewrites, and hierarchical-linkage steering was weaker and more selective; the results therefore do not establish a general, prompt-independent account of refusal (R2, R8, R10–R12).
